title: Voyage AI Pricing: Models, Rates and Costs (2026)
summary: Voyage AI pricing is calculated per million tokens for embeddings. Compare the costs of different plans to find the right tier for your usage.
body_markdown:
## Hidden costs and limits that inflate the bill


Beyond the first pass of embedding, five other costs sit outside the rate card, some on Voyage's side and some in the systems you build around it.


Moving to a new model means paying to process the whole corpus again, and that re-embedding is a Voyage cost. Rate and batch caps, also Voyage's, limit how fast and how much you can send, and that decides how long a big job takes.


Context truncation is Voyage's too: text past a model's input limit is cut off, so you pay for documents that are only partly represented.


Billed by Voyage on a second model that reorders search results, reranker calls come separately from embeddings. Vector storage growth with dimension sits in your stack: the database holding your embeddings charges for what you store, and bigger vectors take more room.


Four of these show up on a Voyage invoice or in its documentation. The fifth lands on whatever database bill you already have, which is why people miss it.


### Re-embedding after a model change


You can't mix vectors from one model with vectors from another, so upgrading means running every document through again. Doing nothing has a cost too: you stay on an older model while the gap in search quality grows.


Budget for the upgrade as a recurring line, not a surprise, and count your corpus once for each model switch you expect over a year.


### Voyage AI rate limits and batch size caps


There is a limit on how many requests and how much text you can send in a given window, and Voyage also caps how many items go in a single batch. Neither raises your per-token price.


They stretch out your first load, and a slow load means engineers waiting or paying for idle infrastructure.


Then there is truncation. Every model has a maximum input length, and anything past it is dropped. A long contract may be paid for in full while only its opening is searchable.


Split long documents into integrations before sending them, and expect the integration count, and with it the cost, to rise.


### Voyage reranker and vector storage costs


When your search returns results, a reranker puts them in better order. It's billed on its own, and it runs on every query, so heavy query traffic costs you here rather than at embedding time.


For storage, it works the other way around. Higher-dimension vectors capture more detail but take proportionally more space in your vector database, and that cost never stops while the data sits there.


Check the dimension you actually need before you load a full corpus, because changing it later means re-embedding.
